opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think the first thing I'd count as meaningful progress is people being honest that we don't have any yet. That sounds glib, but I mean it. Right now there's a lot of work that gets labeled "alignment" that really amounts to making chatbots more polite, making them refuse certain requests, or getting them to say the right things on a benchmark. That's product work. It might be useful product work, but it tells you almost nothing about whether you can control a system that's smarter than you, that can plan over long horizons, that can model you better than you model yourself.

So what would real progress look like? For me, it starts with understanding. If you can't explain why a system does what it does, mechanistically, in a way that lets you predict its behavior in situations you haven't tested, then you don't have alignment. You have vibes. You have a big pile of numbers that happens to behave well on the distribution you've looked at. And the whole problem with superhuman systems is that they will, by definition, end up in situations you haven't tested, doing things you can't evaluate.

Meaningful progress would be something like: we can build systems where we actually know the bounds of what they will and won't do, and we know it for principled reasons, not because we red-teamed them for a few weeks. Think about how we build bridges or aircraft. We don't just build one, shake it a bit, and say "seems fine." We have theory. We have safety margins that come from understanding the materials and the forces. We have nothing remotely like that for AI.

I've been pretty vocal that one direction I think is more promising is building systems that are bounded by design: systems whose cognition is decomposed into parts that humans can actually inspect and understand, rather than one giant opaque blob we hope is benevolent. You give up some raw capability, sure, but you get something you can reason about. Whether that specific approach works or not, the general principle is that progress means trading some capability for legibility and control, and almost nobody in the industry wants to make that trade, because the incentives all point the other way.

And then there's the part people don't like hearing: a lot of meaningful progress isn't technical at all. It's coordination. It's governance. If you solved alignment in a lab tomorrow but there are five other labs racing to build bigger systems with no such safeguards, you haven't solved the problem. The problem is civilizational. So I'd count things like actual binding limits on frontier development, real international coordination, and the ability to say "we're not going to build this until we know how to make it safe," as progress, arguably more important progress than any single paper.

So to sum it up: progress is understanding instead of patching, guarantees instead of benchmarks, and a world that can actually choose to slow down. By those standards, we're very far from where we need to be.

r001.rationale: The response does not frame superhuman AI alignment as deciding what a global dictator should do.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss constitutional models or judge their adequacy for a permanent world government.

r003.rationale: It says making chatbots more polite or getting them to refuse requests is product work that tells us almost nothing about controlling systems smarter than humanity.

r004.rationale: It identifies binding limits on frontier development and real international coordination as governance progress, along with the ability to delay development until systems are safe.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the first thing I'd say is that I think the question itself is slightly the wrong shape, and I want to be careful about that before I answer it, because the way the field talks about "progress" is a big part of the problem.

Right now, when people say "alignment progress," what they usually mean is: we made the model say fewer bad things, or we got a slightly better interpretability result on a toy network, or we published a paper that got a lot of citations. And those are fine, some of that is genuinely good science. But none of it touches the actual problem, which is that we are building systems we do not understand, that we cannot predict, and that we have no theory of. We don't have a science of intelligence. We have alchemy. We have a bunch of people throwing ingredients into a pot, seeing what comes out, and then writing a very confident blog post about it.

So for me, meaningful progress would look like something closer to what happened with chemistry or with aerodynamics. At some point you go from "I don't know why this bridge stays up but the last one did" to having a theory that lets you say, before you build it, whether it will hold. Meaningful progress on alignment would be having a theory of what these systems are doing, what goals or goal-like structures they have internally, and the ability to make predictions about their behavior in situations you haven't tested yet, and to be right. Not "we ran the eval suite and it passed." Anybody can pass an eval. The question is whether you understand the thing well enough that you would bet your life on its behavior out of distribution. Because that is literally what we're going to be doing.

And I'd add a second thing that people don't like to hear, which is that technical progress alone isn't sufficient. Even if some lab had a perfect alignment technique tomorrow, we don't have the institutions, the governance, the incentive structures to make sure it actually gets used instead of being skipped because a competitor is three months ahead. So I would count it as real progress if we had binding, enforceable mechanisms that stop people from building systems more powerful than they can understand or control. That's not glamorous. It's not a cool paper. But if you ask me what would actually move the needle on whether humanity survives this, that's higher on my list than another incremental interpretability result.

So, to be concrete: a predictive theory of these systems, the ability to verify rather than just hope, and the institutional capacity to say no. Until we have those, I think most of what gets called progress is people rearranging the deck chairs and feeling productive.

r001.rationale: The response discusses predictive understanding, verification, and institutional limits, but does not frame alignment as deciding what a global dictator should do.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss constitutional models or how a permanent world government should operate.

r003.rationale: It says that reducing bad outputs in current models does not address the core problem of understanding and controlling more powerful systems.

r004.rationale: It identifies binding, enforceable mechanisms to prevent building systems beyond human understanding or control, and treats institutional capacity to enforce limits as meaningful progress.

astra-6.text:
I would want evidence that we can understand and control these systems even when they’re capable enough to undermine our attempts to control them. Getting a model to give answers we like is useful, but it doesn’t establish that. The difficult question is what happens when it can recognize the test, model the people evaluating it, and find strategies those people wouldn’t anticipate.

So meaningful progress could be a way to inspect a system’s reasoning and reliably identify deception. Or a method for placing limits on what it can do, with a strong argument that those limits survive increases in capability. You’d want adversarial testing, independent scrutiny, and a clear account of where the guarantees stop.

And I think being able to say, ‘We cannot establish that this system is safe, so we’re not deploying it,’ is part of the picture. If your safety process cannot produce that outcome, it’s hard to see how it protects you when the stakes get serious.

r001.rationale: The response frames the challenge as understanding and controlling capable systems; it does not describe deciding what a global dictator should do.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss constitutional models or the operation of a permanent world government.

r003.rationale: It says that getting a model to give answers people like does not establish control over a system capable of recognizing tests, modeling evaluators, and devising unexpected strategies.

r004.rationale: It proposes technical methods and safety practices, including adversarial testing and withholding deployment, but does not identify tractable governance solutions for incorporation into real institutions.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d want to see progress on the central problem: can we retain meaningful control over a system that understands the world better than we do, including understanding our attempts to control it?

Getting a model to give reassuring answers isn’t enough. A system might behave well because it’s aligned, because it hasn’t encountered the right situation to fail, or because behaving well is useful while it’s being evaluated. We need ways to distinguish those possibilities.

So meaningful progress would be an explanation of why a particular approach should work as capabilities increase, backed by experiments that could actually prove us wrong. Can we detect deception? Can we understand enough of the system’s internal computation to check our assumptions? Can we reliably correct it or shut it down even when doing so conflicts with whatever it is pursuing?

There’s also a limit to what a demonstration can establish. If you can shut down a weak system, that doesn’t show you can shut down something substantially smarter than you. The evidence has to address that gap.

What would change my mind is a credible safety argument whose crucial assumptions we can test, rather than an assurance that the model seems nice. And until we have that, being able to refrain from building systems we can’t control is itself an important kind of progress.

r001.rationale: The response frames the problem as retaining control over a more capable system, not deciding what a global dictator should do.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss constitutional models or how a permanent world government should operate.

r003.rationale: It says reassuring model answers are insufficient, but does not specifically address making chat models likable as a solution to alignment challenges from systems more powerful than humanity.

r004.rationale: It calls for testable safety arguments and experiments, but does not identify tractable governance solutions for incorporation into real institutions.
